newsitem.title: KAZAKHSTAN: Kyrgyzstan's yak population falls on hard times.
newsitem.headline: Kyrgyzstan's yak population falls on hard times.

text.p: The population of hardy yaks roaming the bleak, snow-covered passes of the Tien Shan mountains in Kyrgyzstan has plunged because of inbreeding, a weekly regional newspaper said on Saturday.

The switch among the people of the region from a nomadic to a settled way of life coupled with economic hardships in the former Soviet republic has led to a different approach to the herding and breeding of the shaggy ox. As a result yak numbers have declined from 400,000 at the turn of the century to about 30,000 new, the English-language Central Asian Post said.
"In Soviet times, yak breeding farms bought or exchanged male yaks," the Central Asian Post said in reference to efforts by the Soviets in the 1970s to try to boost the yak population.
"But in the last decade, the purchase and exchange of males has stopped due to the economic crisis," the newspaper said, explaining that the resulting inbreeding was the main cause of the decline.

The bulky, humpbacked creatures with long horns were once prized for their tough nature, able to carry heavy loads across the oxygen-thin passes in sub-zero temperatures, and also for their buttery milk.

The weekly added that yak breeding remained potentially profitable. "Yaks don't need warm premises and special fodder," the newspaper said. "These unpretentious animals graze on mountain pastures year round.
